Images, saints, and Mary

Reformed sources · Reformed and Orthodox sources on worship

Images, saints, and Mary

7 sectionsNot completed
Notes

Images, honor toward saints, and the title Mother of God raise several distinct questions. Westminster’s standards, St. John of Damascus, and Piper do not take identical positions even where they discuss the same commandment or biblical event. The Incarnation—the Word truly becoming human—is especially important to the arguments about images of Jesus.[1][2][3][4][5][6]

What does the Larger Catechism forbid?[1]

The Westminster Larger Catechism places representations of any divine person among the things forbidden by the second commandment. It also rejects worship through such representations and religious worship invented without divine institution. This statement is broader than a prohibition limited to worshipping pagan gods.[1]

Read original passage

Westminster: images

109. What are the sins forbidden in the second commandment? A. The sins forbidden in the second commandment are, all devising, counselling, commanding, using, and anywise approving, any religious worship not instituted by God himself; the making any representation of God, of all or of any of the three persons, either inwardly in our mind, or outwardly in any kind of image or likeness of any creature whatsoever; all worshipping of it, or God in it or by it; the making of any representation of feigned deities, and all worship of them, or service belonging to them, all superstitious devices, corrupting the worship of God, adding to it, or taking from it, whether invented and taken up of ourselves, or received by tradition from others, though under the title of antiquity, custom, devotion, good intent, or any other pretence whatsoever; simony; sacrilege; all neglect, contempt, hindering, and opposing the worship and ordinances which God hath appointed.

How does Westminster relate worship and mediation?[2]

Westminster reserves religious worship for God alone. It also identifies Christ alone as mediator. These are the confession’s own boundaries concerning worship, angels, and saints.[2]

Read original passage

Westminster Confession of Faith

Religious worship is to be given to God, the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost; and to him alone; not to angels, saints, or any other creature: and, since the fall, not without a Mediator; nor in the mediation of any other but of Christ alone.

How does St. John relate images to the Incarnation?[3]

St. John distinguishes the invisible, formless divine nature from the real human life of the Word. Christ’s earthly events were visible and can be remembered through accounts of them. This is the basis of the selected argument about depiction.[3]

Read original passage

John of Damascus: images and the Incarnation

But besides this who can make an imitation of the invisible, incorporeal, uncircumscribed, formless God? Therefore to give form to the Deity is the height of folly and impiety. And hence it is that in the Old Testament the use of images was not common. But after God in His bowels of pity became in truth man for our salvation, not as He was seen by Abraham in the semblance of a man, nor as He was seen by the prophets, but in being truly man, and after He lived upon the earth and dwelt among men, worked miracles, suffered, was crucified, rose again and was taken back to Heaven, since all these things actually took place and were seen by men, they were written for the remembrance and instruction of us who were not alive at that time in order that though we saw not, we may still, hearing and believing, obtain the blessing of the Lord.

Where does Piper’s position differ?[4]

Piper allows artistic representations of Jesus because Jesus truly appeared as a human being. The panel answer distinguishes that judgment from his objection to depicting the Father. His permission for pictures or film does not itself establish the Orthodox teaching about honoring icons.[4]

Read original passage

Piper: images of the incarnate Christ

In other words, I don’t think the commandment says you shouldn’t look on the face of Christ, because otherwise all the people who heard him say, “If you’ve seen me, you’ve seen the Father” (John 14:9), would be breaking the second commandment. Therefore, the incarnation, to me, is the legitimization of drawing pictures of Jesus or making a movie with Jesus. I wouldn’t favor drawing pictures of God the Father. If you’re going to draw a picture of the Holy Spirit, it should be a dove.

By John Piper. © Desiring God Foundation. Source: desiringGod.org
